title: Law of Cosines for Sides Checkpoint
description: Show that you can select and use the Law of Cosines to find unknown side lengths in SAS situations.

questions.question: A triangle has sides 8 cm and 13 cm with included angle 52°. Which formula setup finds the opposite side x?
questions.explanation: For SAS, use x² = a² + b² - 2ab cos C, where C is the included angle.

questions.question: Two sides are 8 and 13 with included angle 52°. What is the opposite side to the nearest tenth?
A triangle has two known sides and a non-included angle. Is this the standard SAS setup for finding a side with the Law of Cosines?
options: Yes, any two sides and any angle are SAS.
Yes, because the angle does not matter.
No, SAS requires the included angle.
No, the Law of Cosines cannot use angles.
questions.explanation: SAS means the known angle is between the two known sides. A non-included angle creates a different case.

questions.question: Two sides are 5 and 11 with included angle 130°. What is the opposite side to the nearest tenth?
When the included angle is obtuse, the side opposite that angle is often the longest side.
questions.explanation: A larger angle opens wider, so the side opposite it is longer than the sides opposite smaller angles.

questions.question: For side a, complete the formula: a² = b² + c² - 2bc cos ____.
questions.explanation: Side a is opposite angle A, so the matching formula uses cos A.

questions.question: A hiker walks 4 km, turns through an included angle of 75°, and walks 6 km. What is the direct distance from start to endpoint to the nearest tenth?
A student gets x = -9.8 after solving a Law of Cosines problem. Explain what should be corrected.
questions.correctAnswer: A side length cannot be negative. The student should use the positive square root, so the side length should be 9.8, assuming the setup and arithmetic were correct.
questions.explanation: The formula may involve squared values, but the final side length is a distance, so it must be positive.

questions.question: Which answer is most reasonable for a side opposite a 25° included angle between sides 12 and 14?
questions.explanation: A small included angle usually gives a shorter opposite side. Also, Law of Cosines gives x² = 12² + 14² - 2(12)(14)cos25° ≈ 35.4, so x ≈ 5.9.

questions.question: In one or two sentences, explain how to decide whether a missing-side problem should use the Law of Cosines instead of the Pythagorean Theorem.
questions.correctAnswer: Use the Pythagorean Theorem only when the triangle has a right angle. If the problem gives two sides and the included angle in an oblique triangle, use the Law of Cosines.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is whether a 90° angle is present; Law of Cosines handles the general SAS oblique case.
